analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on January 4, 2021 and no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, and replace them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly all goods and services, collected mainly by the states. Every lawful-resident family would receive a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending. It would also stop funding the IRS after 2025, and the sales tax would expire if the constitutional amendment allowing an income tax were not repealed within seven years.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment income and estates gain the most, since the bill eliminates taxes on capital gains, dividends, and inherited wealth and exempts investment purchases and securities from the sales tax. Businesses gain from untaxed business purchases and the end of income tax compliance. Families near the poverty line gain from the monthly rebate that covers the tax on poverty-level consumption.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: Repeals federal income taxes, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, replacing them with a single 23% national sales tax starting in 2023.
Exempts purchases made for business, investment, or export purposes from the sales tax, and excludes intangible property such as securities, bonds, and financial instruments from the tax base.
Repeals the estate and gift tax entirely, ending the federal tax on large inheritances.

Provides every qualified lawful-resident family a monthly sales tax rebate (the Family Consumption Allowance) equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty guideline for their family size, paid by the Social Security Administration.
Funds Social Security and Medicare from general revenue after repealing the payroll taxes that currently finance them, and allocates sales tax revenue to their trust funds.
Shifts collection to the states, which keep a 0.25% administration fee, and pays registered sellers an administrative credit of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, whichever is greater.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay the new 23% tax on nearly everything they buy, on top of existing state sales taxes. Because households with lower and middle incomes spend nearly all of what they earn, while much of high earners' income goes into savings, investments, and untaxed securities, a consumption tax takes a larger share of income from ordinary families' budgets. The monthly rebate shields only poverty-level spending; income above that is fully taxed at the register while wages, capital gains, and estates face no federal tax at all.

drawbacks.text: A 23% national sales tax would be stacked on the state sales taxes most states already levy, raising combined tax rates at the checkout far above what any state charges today.

The bill exempts investment purchases, securities, and intangible property from the tax and repeals the estate tax, so the tax burden shifts away from wealth and onto consumption — and because lower-income families spend a larger share of their income, the burden falls proportionally harder on them.

The rebate covers only poverty-level consumption; a working family earning modestly above the poverty line pays the full 23% on every dollar it spends with no offsetting income tax cut, since the income tax is repealed.

No funding is authorized for IRS operations after fiscal year 2025, ending federal enforcement of the repealed taxes with no stated mechanism for collecting income taxes owed under them or addressing past evasion.

The sales tax automatically sunsets after seven years if the Sixteenth Amendment (authorizing the income tax) is not repealed, requiring a constitutional amendment that has never come close to passage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The simplification is real: no annual income tax filing, no payroll withholding, and no estate tax planning. But the design trades a progressive tax system — where rates rise with income and large estates are taxed — for a flat consumption tax that taxes every purchase at the same rate. The prebate protects families at the poverty line, but everyone above it pays substantially more of their income in tax, while the households with the largest investment portfolios and estates see their federal tax burden largely disappear. The revenue math also depends on a rate that the bill adjusts in later years, so the true burden on consumers could rise.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Earl L. 'Buddy' Carter (R-GA) introduced the FairTax Act of 2021 on January 4, 2021.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, and the action history records no hearing, markup, or vote after that referral.
Thirty House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing tax system stayed in place, so households that would have paid the new 23% sales tax on nearly everything they buy were spared it, and the estate tax and taxes on capital income remained. The bill's main beneficiaries — large estates and high-investment households — gained nothing, because it never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households spared the new consumption tax

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 4, 2021 and took no recorded action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. Richard Neal
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill during the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 30 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill died without action in the Ways and Means Committee controlled by Democrats; no Democrat cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill repeals the estate tax and all taxes on capital income and exempts investment purchases and securities from the sales tax, so the wealthiest households' federal tax burden largely disappears. The offset is a 23% tax on consumption that takes a larger share of income from ordinary families, who spend nearly everything they earn.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax ends annual filing, the core business of paid preparers and tax software companies. The public gains the same simplification the industry loses, though the new consumption tax creates its own burdens.

Retailers must register, collect, and remit the 23% federal tax at the register and post security bonds if large, but receive an administrative credit of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, whichever is greater. The tax raises checkout prices for their customers, which could dampen sales.
States with existing sales taxes become the primary collectors of the federal tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, locking in a permanent federal collection role for state tax agencies.
